title: The robot's cartwheel was a human's first

beats: This robot just did a cartwheel. A human did it first.
Researchers at Berkeley and Stanford suited people up and recorded them moving: walking, running, dancing, martial arts, cartwheels. About two and a half hours in all.
Then a Unitree G1 humanoid had to follow along. It earns points for matching the move, and loses them for jerky motion, bad joint angles, or bumping into itself.
The moves get squeezed into a compact code, and an AI plans new sequences from it. Sprints. Spin kicks. Flips. Cartwheels.
On the real robot, joystick steering and dodging obstacles worked without retraining.
Does it look human? People compared its walk with Unitree's standard controller. More than two thirds of the time, they picked the new one as more natural.
Boston Dynamics and the RAI Institute built a similar system, ZEST. It learns from mocap, ordinary video, or an animator's keyframes. Even a four-legged robot learned a backflip.
The catch, per ZEST's authors: flat, non-slippery floors only, and nothing it hasn't seen.
Every robot flip starts as someone's dance. Whose motion is it? Tell me below. Follow for the next AI story.
